H1.text: Lemon juice tastes sour. Soap feels slippery. Mix an acid and a base, and you get a salt.

H2.text: For years, chemists asked one question. What exactly makes an acid an acid?

H3.text: Aarav washes his bicycle with soapy water. It feels slippery on his hands.

H4.text: At lunch, a squeeze of lemon tastes sour. Opposites, but why?

H5.text: By the end, you will know three ideas of acids and bases, each bigger than the last.

P2.text: Acids taste sour and turn blue litmus red.

P3.text: Bases taste bitter, feel soapy, and turn red litmus blue.

P4.text: When they meet, they cancel each other and make a salt and water. Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide make common salt.

S1.text: Idea one, from Svante Arrhenius. Let's drop hydrochloric acid into water on our molecule bench.

S2.text: It splits into ions. An ion is an atom with a charge. Here, a hydrogen ion and a chloride ion.

S3.text: So an acid gives hydrogen ions in water.

S4.text: But a hydrogen ion is just a bare proton. It is too small to stay alone. It grabs a water molecule and becomes a hydronium ion, H three O plus.

S5.text: A base, like sodium hydroxide, gives hydroxide ions, O H minus, in water.

S6.text: The weak spot. It only works in water. And ammonia has no O H, yet it is a base.

L1.text: Idea two, from Bronsted and Lowry, in nineteen twenty three. Think of passing a ball.

L2.text: An acid is a proton giver. A base is a proton taker.

L3.text: So an acid base reaction is just one proton passing from one particle to another.

D1.text: Let's follow one proton, step by step.

D3.text: Step two. Water gives a proton to ammonia. Water is the acid. Ammonia is the base.

D4.text: Step three. Ammonia becomes ammonium, N H four plus. Water becomes hydroxide, O H minus.

D5.text: Step four. Run it backward. Ammonium can give the proton back, so it is an acid. Hydroxide can take it, so it is a base.

G1.text: These partners have a name. Conjugate pairs.

G2.text: A conjugate pair differs by just one proton.

G3.text: Ammonia and ammonium are one pair. Water and hydroxide are the other.

G4.text: A strong acid gives away its proton easily. So its partner, the conjugate base, is weak.

G5.text: Water can act as an acid or as a base. We call it amphoteric.

C1.text: Compare. With ammonia, water gives a proton, so it is an acid. With hydrochloric acid, water takes a proton, so it is a base.

K1.text: Pause and think. When H C l gives its proton to water, what is left behind as the conjugate base?

K2.text: Chloride. Take one proton away from H C l, and you get C l minus.

R1.text: Idea three, from G N Lewis, also in nineteen twenty three. Not every reaction passes a proton.

R2.text: Lewis looked at electron pairs instead. A Lewis base gives an electron pair. A Lewis acid takes one.

R3.text: Boron trifluoride is short of electrons. Ammonia has a lone pair, a pair not used in any bond.

R4.text: Ammonia shares its pair with boron, and a new bond forms. Boron trifluoride is the Lewis acid. Ammonia is the Lewis base.

R5.text: Electron short particles like aluminium chloride and the magnesium ion are Lewis acids. Water, ammonia and hydroxide are Lewis bases.

T1.text: Remember this. Bronsted is about protons. Lewis is about electron pairs.

W2.text: Find the conjugate base of three acids. H F, sulphuric acid, and the hydrogen carbonate ion.

W3.text: The rule. Take away one proton, and lower the charge by one.

W4.text: H F loses a proton. Its conjugate base is fluoride, F minus.

W5.text: Sulphuric acid, H two S O four, becomes H S O four minus. Hydrogen carbonate, H C O three minus, becomes carbonate, C O three two minus.

W6.text: Going the other way, add one proton. The conjugate acid of ammonia is ammonium.

X2.text: Students take away the hydrogen, but forget to change the charge.

X3.text: A proton carries a plus charge. Remove it, and the charge drops by one. H C O three minus becomes C O three two minus.

E1.text: Where is this asked? Boards ask for conjugate acids and bases, and to sort Lewis acids from bases. Entrance tests ask which particle is a Lewis acid but not a Bronsted acid.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Which of these is a Lewis acid, but not a Bronsted acid? A, the ammonium ion. B, boron trifluoride. C, water. D, H C l. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Boron trifluoride.

A2.text: It has no hydrogen to give, so it cannot be a Bronsted acid.

A3.text: But boron has room for an electron pair, so it is a Lewis acid.

A4.text: Ammonium, water and H C l can all give a proton. They are Bronsted acids.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. What does a Bronsted base do?

Y3.text: Two. Write the conjugate base of H two S O four.

Y4.text: Three. Why is boron trifluoride a Lewis acid?

N1.text: Next time: even pure water splits a tiny bit into ions. How do we measure that? We find out in Ionization of Water and the pH Scale.
